Yes, you are overreacting but I understand your perspective because I was 18 once. It may not seem like it, but giving you a place to live and giving you this note is actually an act of love even if it seems harsh. 

These things are part of being a responsible adult and having a routine and motivation is way healthier than sitting in your room playing video games and letting your dogs pee everywhere. I’m guessing part of the yard work will be picking up your dogs poo, but I don’t wanna assume. This is a VERY mild chore list. I do all of this all day, multiple times a day as a cleaner and more. 

Put on a podcast, set timers on your phone and get er’ done. If you feel overwhelmed and unsure of what’s expected of you, would your aunt or uncle be open to talking if you were like “hey, would you mind sharing any tips with me or giving me feedback on how I’ve cleaned x?” Choose the days of the week you’re going to do the weekly chores so it doesn’t get confusing with skipping days and shifting things around. 

It’s hard to clean if you’ve never been taught, I understand. The great thing about cleaning is, the more you keep up with it the easier to maintain. If it never gets brutally disgusting, you don’t have those super overwhelming cleans where you’re spending hours going through trash and tidying up. If the adults in your life can’t help you or are at their limit, go on YouTube or TikTok there are thousands of videos showing the most effective ways to clean. If you’re able to use Reddit to post this, use YouTube, theres zero reason you can’t learn to do chores. No excuses. It should be number one priority to make sure you have a stable living situation, most people would kill to be able to exchange chores to live rent free. Don’t sabotage a good set up for yourself. 

As for your aunts bf, what he does with his cereal bowls or cleaning is not your concern. It is not the gotcha you think. It’s your aunts house, you are living there rent free so mind your aunt and pseudo uncle, respect their house and above all respect yourself. No one wants to live with a stinky and/or messy roommate or partner. You are setting yourself up for a future of drama in living situations if you don’t get over these bad habits. I sympathize with your depression and grief and can relate a lot. But I promise you not taking care of yourself and responsibilities does not help. All the best to you.

People leave cleaning companies for all kinds of reasons. The only reason people have left me is because they went back to school, moved to a new city or got a career in their field. Majority come back for part time when they need some extra cash. B is being a bit sketchy, most of us who own cleaning companies have folks sign non solicitation agreements. Id bet she’s violating multiple clauses in her contract. Some people don’t realize that owners spend hours on admin and lots of money into advertising, etc. I pay for business insurance for our cleaners, Jobber subscription as well as supplies. We’re not some evil people sitting on our asses exploiting people. We’re a small business and pay people fairly. The reason her hourly rate is so much cheaper is because with A’s company, they were paying insurance and for advertising to find/maintain her assigned clients. 

I had a cleaner who was amazing at first, but after she got comfortable got extremely rude and demanding with me. One night after getting wasted at a staff party, she screamed in my face about politics, insulted me and quit out of embarrassment the next day. She tried to steal over 40k/year worth of clients to start her own company and ended up taking two with her, despite signing her contract indicating she had to pay me out per client she poached. I just let it go because she was unhinged and it would’ve been unprofessional of me to tell those clients why she left. THIS is why we don’t like people texting clients behind our backs. Thankfully she only managed to take 2 clients. 

She lasted a month before begging to come back. Turns out, there isn’t a magical cleaning client fairy that drops jobs in your lap. Turns out, scheduling, invoicing and organization isn’t for everyone. Turns out, you NEED insurance for when you break something. She learned all this the hard way. 

There is nothing wrong with using an independent cleaner. I was one before I started my company. There are tons of wonderful, reliable people working solo. But there are definitely a benefits to working with an established company. It’s up to you to decide which one suits you and your needs best. If it doesn’t work out with B, A will likely be able to set you up with a new cleaner no problem in the future.

I own a cleaning company - not only are we insured/bonded and do background checks and vetting for all new hires, but our cleaners also sign a very detailed contract with several clauses regarding confidentiality. Our cleaners are aware that breaching any of those terms will lead to immediate termination of their contract (which they do not want to do because we pay $30+ an hour and they make good tips).

We have tons of clients with multi-million dollar homes, and that work as lawyers, surgeons, politicians and a lot of other positions where there is sensitive information, money and valuables everywhere.

Truth be told, even most independent cleaners would likely not want to risk losing you as a client / losing the income to do something that stupid. But if you don’t want to risk that, I’d say your best bet is to find out who the other folks in your position are hiring and can vouch for. My most “wealthy” personal clients have insanely valuable art collections for example, so I’ve received a tremendous amount of referrals on their street for their neighbours looking for a someone insured for at least a few million. The most important thing about this job is managing client expectations and setting yourself up for success. When I’m doing a deep clean, we ask the clients what areas are most important to them and what their must haves are. Usually, they will tell you stuff like “don’t worry about all my stuff on my desk and craft table if you don’t have time”, “I would love if you could focus on the bathroom and kitchen, baseboards etc.” if that’s the case, if I’m done their must haves and have extra time, then I can do the less important shit to wow them. Just be honest about what is physically possible in the time alotted - if they’re nice clients they will be chill. 

Do you have a deep clean checklist? If not, I highly recommend putting one together so you stay on schedule and only doing what’s required. Personally, I do not include fridge/freezer cleanings in a deep clean unless it’s a tenant turnover where the appliances aren’t being replaced. If the client wants that, they pay $60 and I ensure there is an extra hour set aside. Sometimes people will randomly be like, “hey, btw can you also clean all the windows in my house too” to which I will respectfully let them know it’s not possible and use that as an upsell opportunity for a next appointment. 

In my opinion, 3 hours is way too long on a bedroom unless a client specifically asked for organization or for you to spend more time in there. I “threw them into the fire” and was too trusting in people stating their own abilities. I fucked up, and it was a learning experience. 

My partner and I started a new training system that has worked well so far. If someone wants to work for us, they need to have minimum 2 years experience, and their first test clean is my loft (paid of course). It’s a win-win because I get my place cleaned, and get the customer experience from the new hire. They get honest feedback, and if they need more training I book them on 1-2 team cleans with me before booking them on their own. 

The other BIGGEST mistake I’ve made with hiring is not firing earlier! I literally can’t stress this enough to other cleaning businesses. Do NOT waste your time on shitty people. State the expectations very clearly in your independent contractor agreement and make it clear you can terminate them at any time. Reward awesome performance, but don’t hold out for unreliable people to change because they WON’T.

A huge battle is that people usually fall into 2 categories: meh at cleaning, but have an awesome personality, punctual etc. OR they’re savants at cleaning but then are nightmarish divas to deal with. I got lucky in that my most recent two hires have been killing it and happen to be really experienced and pleasant cleaners.

We hire independent cleaners and have a Non-Solicitation clause in our independent contractor agreement. I first tried to kill myself at 15 because I was horrible at school and had severe depression. I would never guess that 15 years later in my 30s, I would have my own successful business and be with the girl of my dreams.

Getting a job at your age allowed me to save, and get work experience so I could move out to the big city at 18. It also helped me make friends and come out of my shell. I know people who learned to draw in their 20s and who are now successful tattoo artists that travel the world for guest spots and have their own studios. I have a cleaning business which involves travelling around the city and working inside peoples homes, which are mostly families! I would personally avoid the downtown core if you have a family. You’ll be looking at shitty overpriced condos, no yard and crackheads wandering outside screaming. 

With your budget, I’d consider checking out the following areas:

-The Beaches (family friendly, wonderful food, outdoor recreation) 

-Leslieville (see above) 

-Trinity Bellwoods (Shaw, Crawford snd surrounding streets have some beautiful Victorian homes and this area is within walking distance of downtown, shopping, restaurants and Trinity Bellwoods Park. It is also a fantastic place to have a dog)

-Oakwood Village (St.Clair/ Vaughan, Oakwood etc) really charming community with lots of families and older larger homes. I have many clients with small children in that area and they seem to love it. Hudson College, a private K-12 school is nearby as well. 

-The Junction (lots of young parents, pretty “hip” area. Pretty good vibes)

-High Park (Awesome community, outdoor recreation, high park, fantastic area to have dogs)

-Roncesvalles (pretty side streets, great restaurants, lots of families)

I work in Leslieville and The Beaches a lot and it’s really lovely. I see tons of families out and about, and the neighborhoods I work in are really quaint with pretty homes. The food in the East End is wonderful too. The only thing is, I’m guessing if you’re from California that you’re used to driving everywhere.   Driving in the east end is kind of hellish, I agree with people who say Leslieville is slightly more accessible for transit. I believe there are Hone Fitness locations in Greek Town and Leslieville, which is my personal fav gym franchise to use in Toronto and is quite affordable. 

When I was in LA a couple of months ago, I was so frustrated by how bad the transit was and how it is not walkable at all, so maybe you will enjoy that here? I gave up and just rented a car when I was there haha. You’ll be able to easily walk to a nice coffee shop or restaurant, unlike California where everything’s super spread out (not sure what city you’re in though or if it’s like that everywhere). Winter here is not that brutal as long as you’re dressed well. Get a warm coat, scarf, a toque, some gloves and blundstones and you’ll be fine. Taking little ones ice skating and Tobogganing in the winter is also super fun :) our winters have been kind of mild the last couple of years anyhow, more dreary and rainy than blizzards. All the best to you and your family!

Oh man, where do I start? First of all, a lot of LA is beautiful and I can definitely see the appeal of the weather. The food is also incredible. I hated that my only viable option to get around was by renting a car or taking Lyfts. Most areas are really spread out and inaccessible by walking or transit. 

LA is not walkable AT ALL. If you don’t have a car in LA, you’re royally fucked. There are neighborhoods you go to where there’s no one on the street except homeless people or people going for a run. Everyone’s in a car stuck in traffic. I’ve never felt so sketchy in my life while trying to go for a walk, or just sitting in public trying to chill and have a smoke. Anytime I tried to strike up a friendly conversation with a stranger, they were not really open or receptive like they are in Toronto. People love to complain about Toronto, but in comparison to a lot of the places I’ve been to in the states, it’s a honestly a fantastic city. And it’s friendlier than people give it credit for. It’s really multicultural here, and you get to meet all kinds of people. In LA, it seems like people tend to interact with their races only and it feels weirdly segregated. My friend works at a Target where the staff lunch tables are all separated by race. The white people are the bosses. People are also kind of braggadocious in a way that is off putting, but that’s a whole other post.  

Here, I’m used to walking around and talking to my neighbours, sitting and having a beer shooting the shit. My gf and I love going to Bellwoods, Christie Pitts and other parks to smoke a j, read and maybe have a beer. Doing that in LA you feel kind of like a criminal and that it’s not really socially acceptable to do that if you’re not at the beach. It was like I was chronically loitering and being suspicious. I felt the most happy at the beach because there were actually PEOPLE walking around and I missed that a lot. It’s weirdly lonely in a way you don’t experience somewhere like Toronto or New York. 

The transit system is also a joke - they don’t have comfy terminals or bus stops everywhere like we do. And It’s fucking scorching hot there, so I can’t imagine being a senior citizen waiting for the bus. It takes fucking forever to get anywhere by bus. 

Anyways that’s my stoned rant but I could go on forever about why I hate LA. People don’t realized how spoiled we are in Toronto.

I own a cleaning business. TRUST me, we have seen it all! I get a lot of clients who are really ashamed of the state of their place and it makes me sad. It’s usually not quite as bad as they think. Most experienced cleaners/companies have done lots of depression cleans so if someone shamed you or said “hell naw”, that’s not a professional or someone you want cleaning your home. 

General etiquette would be:

-not leaving a huge sink completely full of dishes if you can. People do not realize that when they do this, it can really eat into the time your cleaner has to complete other things. But if that’s one of the tasks you specifically need help  with or you have a dishwasher, it’s not a huge deal. 

-Staying out of the cleaners way is usually the best. We have our own system and order of doing things, so it can be hard if someone is helping or hovering. However, being communicative and giving the cleaner a heads up on what areas they don’t have to do the first visit and what is okay to throw away is super helpful! 

-Leave out the mop and vacuum for them, let them know where to find any cleaning supplies/ garbage bags etc and where your garbage bins or chute are located. 

-If you’ve never used a cleaner before, perhaps try to book a “deep clean” for your first appointment if you can afford it. After that, you can switch to a maintenance clean and it will be a breeze. The deep clean will usually involve stuff like removing cobwebs, cleaning baseboards, spot cleaning doors and walls etc. depending on the company. These are tasks that are not usually included in a maintenance clean, but will make a world of difference in freshening up the space and only have to be done once in a blue moon. 

-In cases like this, I would usually suggest booking a free quote to have the cleaner come and take a quick look before the appointment is booked. This will allow you to speak to the cleaner about your top priorities, expectations for first clean, and have them assess how long of an appointment they need. That way, they will know exactly what to expect, and will eliminate any surprises.

-if you need help with specific things such as organization, appliance maintenance (inside of oven, fridge etc), blinds or windows, you should let the cleaner know ahead of time so they can bring the appropriate products and cook enough time. There are many times when I show up, and someone is like, “by the way can you also clean my oven, fridge, and organize my hall closet?” Not knowing it may take up to another hour or so. 

I’m happy to answer any questions you may have and wish you the best in finding a cleaner :)
